main.text: [III, 352] Chapter X. [col. 502]

The name and origin of bees. How they are read to have been found in the lion's carcass. That they hear, are frightened by the ringing of brass, are driven out by smoke, and are remarkable for their bravery, on various passages of Scripture.

The Hebrew דבר means not only to speak but also to order, to rule, to lead, to lead down, following the usage of the Chaldeans. For examples see 1 Sam 8:21. Ps 47:4 and XVIII, 48. Hence the bee is called in Hebrew דברה debora, in Chaldee דברא dabbara, from its wonderful guidance and order; just as in Arabic دبر [dbr] dabron is a swarm of bees ^{R1}. For this little creature is a political one, having kings, peoples, [III, 353] cities and palaces. On these, among the Greeks, the chief authorities to consult are Aristotle, Aelian and the writers of the Geoponica; among the Romans, Varro, Virgil, Columella, Pliny; and among the Arabs, Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] and Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]. I have no leisure to plunder their book-chests on so well-worn a subject.

That bees are generated not only from bees but also from an ox is a constant report among writers. Antigonus, Account of Marvels 23: Ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ τὸν βοῦν ἐὰν κατορύξῃς ἐν τόποις τισὶν, ὥστε αὐτὰ τὰ κέρατα τῆς γῆς ὑπερέχειν, εἶθ᾽ ὕστερον ἀποπρίσῃς, λέγουσιν μελίττας ἐκπέτεσθαι· σαπέντα γὰρ αὐτὸν εἰς τοῦτο διαλύεσθαι τὸ ζῶον [En Aigyptō ton boun ean katoryxēs en topois tisin, hōste auta ta kerata tēs gēs hyperechein, eith᾽ hysteron apopris ēs, legousin melittas ekpetesthai; sapenta gar auton eis touto dialyesthai to zōon]. In some places of Egypt, if you bury an ox so that the horns stand above the ground, and then saw them off, they say that bees fly out; for it, when putrefied, is changed into this animal. Varro likewise on the ox, On Agriculture book 2, chapter 5: I know that from it, when putrefied, are born the sweetest [col. 503] bees, the mothers of honey; from which the Greeks call them βουγόνας [bougonas]. And book 3, chapter 16: Bees are born partly from bees, partly from the putrefied body of an ox. Columella, book 1, chapter 4: That bees can be generated from a slain bullock, Democritus and Mago, and no less Virgil, have reported. Mago indeed affirms that the same happens also from the bellies of oxen. Philo, On Those Who Sacrifice: Μέλιττα ζῶόν ἐστιν οὐ καθαρὸν, ἐκ σήψεως καὶ φθορᾶς νεκρῶν, ὡς ὁ λόγος, βοῶν γεννώμενον [Melitta zōon estin ou katharon, ek sēpseōs kai phthoras nekrōn, hōs ho logos, boōn gennōmenon]; The bee is an impure animal, which they say is born from the putrefaction and corruption of dead oxen. Pliny, book 11, chapter 20: There are some who (think) that bees wholly lost are restored by fresh ox bellies covered with dung. Plutarch at the end of the Cleomenes: Μελίττας μὲν βόες, σφῆκας δὲ ἵπποι κατασαπέντες ἐξανθοῦσι [Melittas men boes, sphēkas de hippoi katasapentes exanthousi]; Putrefied oxen put forth bees, and horses wasps. Aelian at the end of book 2: Ἀποθανὼν δὲ βοῦς γενναῖόν τι χρῆμα, καὶ ἀξιέπαινον· μέλιτται γοῦν ἐκ τῶν ἐκείνου λειψάνων ἐκφύονται [Apothanōn de bous gennaion ti chrēma, kai axiepainon; melittai goun ek tōn ekeinou leipsanōn ekphyontai]. Even a dead ox is an excellent thing and to be highly valued, since bees spring from its remains. Galen, in the book Whether What Is Contained in the Womb Is an Animal, chapter 5: Οὐ δὲ γὰρ ὅπως ἐν φυτοῖς σκώληκες γίνονται, ἢ ἀφ᾽ ἵππων καὶ βοῶν οἱ σφῆκες, καὶ μέλιτται, ῥᾴδιον ἡμῖν λέγειν [Ou de gar hopōs en phytois skōlēkes ginontai, ē aph᾽ hippōn kai boōn hoi sphēkes, kai melittai, rhadion hēmin legein]; For neither is it easy for you to say how worms are generated in plants, or wasps and bees from horses and oxen. Origen, Against Celsus [III, 354] book 4: Since we do not marvel that even now a serpent comes from a dead man, from the marrow of the spine, as they say; and a bee from an ox, a wasp from a horse, a beetle from an ass. Servius on book 4 of the Georgics: There are many kinds of bees. Properly, however, those from oxen are called bees, from horses drones, from mules hornets, from asses wasps. And in what way this happens is related at length by Florentinus in book 15 of the Geoponica, chapter [2], Περὶ μελισσῶν, καὶ πῶς ἂν ἐκ βοὸς γένηται ὃ καλεῖται βουγόνη [Peri melissōn, kai pōs an ek boos genētai ho kaleitai bougonē], On bees, and how what is called BUGONE comes from an ox. Many poets agree, as among the Greeks Philetas in Antigonus: the one, namely, whom Suidas attests was the tutor of Ptolemy II and wrote Elegies and Epigrams.
Βουγενέας φάμενος προσεβήσαο μακρὰ μελίσσας, [Bougeneas phamenos prosebēsao makra melissas,] Having spoken thus, you approached from afar the ox-born bees.
And Archelaus in Varro, when he calls bees
— — βοὸς φθιμένης πεποιημένα τέκνα, [boos phthimenēs pepoiēmena tekna,]
the manufactured offspring of a corrupted cow. And the same again,
Ἵππων μὲν σφῆκες γενεαὶ, μόσχων δὲ μέλισσαι· [Hippōn men sphēkes geneai, moschōn de melissai;] Wasps born from horses, but bees from the origin of bulls.
Whom Nicander imitates thus in the Theriaca, line 741.
Ἵπποι γὰρ σφηκῶν γένεσις, ταῦροι δὲ μελισσῶν, Σκήνεσι πυθομένοισι, λυκοσπάδες ἐξεγένοντο· [Hippoi gar sphēkōn genesis, tauroi de melissōn, Skēnesi pythomenoisi, lykospades exegenonto;]

For horses torn by wolves generated wasps, and bulls bees, from their corrupted bodies. (Note in passing that σκῆνος [skēnos], tent, is taken for body, as by Paul 2 Cor 5:1 4.). And Ovid in book 15 of the Metamorphoses,

— — — bury the slaughtered bulls. (A thing known by experience) from the rotting flesh everywhere flower-gathering bees are born, which, after the manner of their parents, tend the fields, are devoted to their work, and labor in hope.
But most fully of all, the prince of poets, in the fourth book of the Georgics [vs. 554 ff.], from which it will suffice to have quoted these few lines:

Here indeed they behold a sudden portent, wondrous to tell: through the dissolved flesh of the oxen, throughout the whole belly, bees buzzing, and swarming out of the burst ribs, and vast clouds trailing, and now at the treetop flowing together, and letting down a cluster from the pliant boughs. [III, 355] Since the ancients report these things about the origin of bees with such agreement, it may seem surprising that we read, in Judges, chapter 14, verse 8, that Samson found עדת דברים, a swarm of bees, in the carcass of the lion. All the more so, since bees are said to abstain from flesh and to flee strong smells altogether. Aristotle, book 9, chapter 40: πρὸς σάρκα δὲ οὐδενὸς καθίζει, οὐδὲ ὀψοφαγεῖ [pros sarka de oudenos kathizei, oude opsophagei]; It settles on the flesh of no [col. 504] animal, nor does it crave cooked dishes. Varro, On Agriculture, book 3, chapter 16: None of them settles on a filthy place, or on one that smells bad. Likewise: They do not lick things as flies do, for no one sees them (as one sees flies) on flesh, or blood, or fat. Pliny, book 11, chapter 21, on wasps and hornets: All feed on flesh, unlike bees, which touch no body. Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] on the bee, chapter 28:
Καὶ ζῇ μὲν ἁγνὸν ἡ σοφὴ σχεδὸν βίον, Ἄγευστος οὖσα νεκρικῶν σπαραγμάτων· [Kai zē men hagnon hē sophē schedon bion, Ageustos ousa nekrikōn sparagmatōn]

And the wise creature leads a chaste life, and does not taste the torn flesh of carcasses. Didymus, Geoponica, book 15 [ch. 2, §. 22]: Ἔστι δὲ καὶ καθαρὸν ὑπερβολῇ τὸ ζῶον, οὐδενὶ τῶν δυσωδῶν καὶ ἀκαθάρτων προσιζάνον, οὔτε λίχνον· οὔτε γὰρ σαρξὶν, οὔτε αἵματι, οὔτε λιπάσματι οὐδενὶ προΐπταται· [Esti de kai katharon hyperbolē to zōon, oudeni tōn dysōdōn kai akathartōn prosizanon, oute lichnon; oute gar sarxin, oute haimati, oute lipasmati oudeni proiptatai] It is also an exceedingly clean animal, settling on nothing foul-smelling or impure, nor greedy (in Greek οὔτε λίχνον [oute lichnon], which others absurdly render nor to the lamp) for it flies neither to flesh, nor to blood, nor to any fat ^{R2}. Indeed, if any bee dies in the hive, the survivors carry the carcass out, lest it give off a foul smell. Virgil:
— — — then the bodies of those bereft of light they carry out of the dwellings, and lead mournful funerals.

Pliny, book 11, chapter 18: They carry out the dead, and accompany the obsequies in the manner of mourners. Aelian, Historia, book 5, chapter 49: Χελιδὼν ἐκβάλλει χελιδόνα νεκρὰν, καὶ μέλιτταν μέλιττα· [Chelidōn ekballei chelidona nekran, kai melittan melitta] A swallow carries out a dead swallow, and a bee a bee. Damir: اذا هلك شي منها داخل الخلايا اخرجته الاحيا خارج [idhā halaka shay minhā dākhil al-khalāyā akhrajathu al-aḥyā khārij] When one of them has died in the hive, the living carry it outside. [III, 356] To these objections that can be raised against the sacred text I have two answers. First, the bees were found in the lion's body, but were not born there; for the author does not assert this. Those therefore are mistaken who on this basis posit a race of bees λεοντογενῶν [leontogenōn], since nowhere in the writings of the ancients do we read that bees are born from a lion. Nor should we listen to Moffett, the Englishman, who in the Insectorum Theatrum writes that some bees are λεοντογενεῖς [leontogeneis], others ταυρογενεῖς [taurogeneis]: namely, that the best and truly noble ones have their origin from the lion, and that their princes and kings derive their lineage from its brain. Hence, he says, it comes about that, small as they are, they sometimes attack the very largest animals and, endowed with leonine ferocity, fear nothing. If this were true, bees would be fiercest in places that teem with lions. But I shall prove without any trouble that the matter is quite otherwise. For in Ethiopia, where Oppian, in book 3 of the Cynegetica, describes those terrible lions from personal observation, bees are so tame that they usually build their nests among the dwellings of men. So Alvarez testifies in his Ethiopia. On the other hand, in Crete ^{a)}, where there are neither lions, nor wolves, nor bears, nor any harmful animal, bees were so fierce that they sometimes drove the inhabitants from their homes, as will be proved below. And in Scythia ^{b)}, which is very far from lions, certain places beyond the Ister were once inaccessible, because bees so occupied them that one could not advance further. Herodotus, book 5, chapter 10, reports that he received this from the Thracians, who live nearest the Ister. He himself, however, rejects it as hardly credible, on the ground that bees seem to be ζῶα δύσριγα [zōa dysriga], animals that cannot endure cold. But many writers refute Herodotus: thus Maximus of Tyre, Oration 2 On Love: Σκυθῶν δὲ οἱ μὲν πολλοὶ γάλακτι βιοτεύουσιν, ὡς οἱ ἄλλοι ἐπὶ οἴνῳ, τοῖς δὲ αἱ μέλιτται καθηδύνουσι τὸ πόμα, ἐπὶ πετρῶν καὶ δρυῶν διαπλάττουσαι τοὺς σίμβλους. [Skythōn de hoi men polloi galakti bioteuousin, hōs hoi alloi epi oinō, tois de hai melittai kathēdynousi to poma, epi petrōn kai dryōn diaplattousai tous simblous.] Most of the Scythians sustain life on milk, just as others do on wine; for others, the bees, which build their honeycombs either on rocks or in oaks, sweeten their drink. And Aelian, book 2, ch. 53: I remember that someone records [col. 505] καὶ μελίττας Σκυθίδας εἶναι, ἐπαΐειν τε τοῦ κρύους οὐδὲν, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ πιπράσκειν εἰς Μυσοὺς κομίζοντας Σκύθας, οὐκ ἐθνεῖον (read ὀθνεῖον) σφίσιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἀνθιγενὲς (read αὐθιγενὲς) μέλι καὶ κηρία ἐπιχώρια [kai melittas Skythidas einai, epaiein te tou kryous ouden, kai men toi kai pipraskein eis Mysous komizontas Skythas, ouk ethneion (read othneion) sphisin, alla anthigenes (read authigenes) meli kai kēria epichōria], that there are bees also in Scythia which are not harmed by the cold, and that the Scythians export honey, not foreign but native, and native honeycombs, for sale to the Mysians. Nor let anyone be indignant with me for writing contrary to Herodotus. For he who writes this has declared that he is presenting history, not repeating uncertain rumour. And Matthias of Miechów, book 2 On European Sarmatia, ch. 1: This is the most fertile of lands, and most productive of grain and honey. Likewise: Swarms of bees make honey not only in hives and hollowed trees, but also deposit honey of their own accord in trees and in the earth. [III, 357] And Paolo Giovio, in his book On the Embassy of the Muscovites: The surest harvest of Muscovy consists in wax and honey. For the whole region is full of most fertile bees, which produce the finest honey not in hives made by the hands of peasants, but in the very hollows of trees. See there the rest, about very large lakes of honey, and about the peasant who, sunk in a pool of honey, was wondrously rescued by a she-bear. For I do not care to linger longer on a very well-known matter.

Second, lest it be asked how Samson's bees could have touched the flesh of a carcass or endured its foul smell, since bees shrink from both, I say that what is here called a carcass was rather a σκελετὸν σῶμα [skeleton sōma], a dried and withered body, in which nothing remained but the framework of the bones. So the Syriac translator takes it, who rendered ܫܠܕܐ ܓܪܡܢܝܐ [שלדא גרמניא], that is, a bony carcass, or, what is the same, a σκελετόν [skeleton]. This interpretation is favoured by the fact that the lion's carcass had lain on the ground for a long time. For Samson, who had killed it, left it lying in the field, וישב מימים, and he returned after days (so it reads literally) to take Delilah, and he turned aside to see the carcass of that lion. After days: that is, after a year. So the Hebrews take it in this passage, and so it is used throughout Scripture. Thus Gen 4:3. And it came to pass מקץ ימים, at the end of days: that is, at the end of a year. Genes. XXIV, 55. Let the girl remain with us ימים או עשר, days, or ten: that is, a year, or ten months. Lev 25:29 If someone sells a house, etc. ימים תהיה גאלתו, for days shall be its redemption: that is, the right of redeeming it shall last for a year, until שנה תמימה, a full year, is completed: as is explained in the following verse. Judg 11:4. And it came to pass after days (that is, after a year) that the Ammonites made war against the Israelites. And vers. 40. מימים ימימה, From days to days (that is, from year to year, in one word annually) the daughters of Israel went to lament the daughter of Jephthah. As in 1 Sam 1:3. That man went up from days to days to worship in Shiloh: that is, שנה בשנה, annually, as is explained in vers. 7. And in vers. 20 of the same chapter: In the revolution of days (that is, of a year) Hannah conceived and bore a son. And II, 19. To offer the sacrifice of days, that is, the yearly one. And XXVII, 7. And the number of days that David dwelt in the country of the Philistines was ימים וארבעה חדשים, days (that is, a year) and four months. Nothing is more frequent than this expression. Therefore, when Samson is said to have returned after days, etc., it is the same as if it were said that only after a year did he return and turn aside to see the carcass of the lion killed a year before ^{R3}. From [III, 358] this it is therefore probable that nothing but the bones remained, since time had consumed the flesh, or wild beasts had devoured it. In such a skeleton, then, why could a swarm of bees not have settled and made its honey, as in the head of Onesilus hung at the gate of Amathus? For so Herodotus has it, book 5, ch. 114: Ὀνησίλου μὲν Ἀμαθούσιοι, ὅτι σφέας ἐπολιόρκησε, ἀποταμόντες τὴν κεφαλὴν, ἐκόμι- [col. 506] σαν εἰς Ἀμαθοῦντα, καὶ μιν ἀπεκρέμασαν ὑπὲρ τῶν πυλέων· κρεμαμένης δὲ τῆς κεφαλῆς, καὶ ἔσης ἤδη κοίλης, ἐσμὸς μελισσέων, ἐσδὺς ἐς αὐτὴν, κηρίων μιν ἐνέπλησε· [Onēsilou men Amathousioi, hoti spheas epoliorkēse, apotamontes tēn kephalēn, ekomisan eis Amathounta, kai min apekremasan hyper tōn pyleōn; kremamenēs de tēs kephalēs, kai esēs ēdē koilēs, esmos melisseōn, esdys es autēn, kēriōn min eneplēse] The Amathusians cut off the head of Onesilus, because he had besieged them, and, having carried it to Amathus, hung it above the gates. And when it, hanging there, had already become hollow, a swarm of bees entered it and filled it with honeycombs. And in the tomb of Hippocrates, if we believe Soranus in his Life, μέχρι πολλοῦ σμῆνος ἦν ἐργαζόμενον μέλι [mechri pollou smēnos ēn ergazomenon meli], there was for a long time a swarm of bees making honey. Nor is it unlike what I have read in Aldrovandi, book 1 On Insects, page 110: that at Verona, in the church of the Holy Cross, in the tomb of the sisters of the distinguished jurist Bartholomaeus Vitalis, one of whom had died in the year 1558 and the other in 1562, bees made honeycombs abundantly between the two carcasses, until in the year 1566 the tomb was opened by lightning, without any damage either to the carcasses or to the honeycombs, and displayed before everyone the honeycombs themselves and the bees making honey in great numbers.

There are those who deny that bees hear. Yet on Isa 7:18. The Lord shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria, Cyril writes thus: Πεποίηται τοίνυν ὁ λόγος, ὡς ἐκ μεταφορᾶς τῆς τῶν μελισσοκόμων ἐμπειρίας, οἳ συρίσμασι τὰς μυίας ἀποφέρον τί τε (read ἀποφέρουσί τε) τῶν σίμβλων εἰς ἀγροὺς, καὶ πάλιν ἀνακομίζουσι· [Pepoiētai toinyn ho logos, hōs ek metaphoras tēs tōn melissokomōn empeirias, hoi syrismasi tas myias apopheron ti te (read apopherousi te) tōn simblōn eis agrous, kai palin anakomizousi] The speech is figurative, a metaphor taken, as it were, from the skill of beekeepers, who by hissing call the flies out of the hives into the fields and lead them back again. And on Isa 5:26. He will hiss for them from the end of the earth, the same Cyril writes: Δέχεται δὲ καὶ τοῦτο πάλιν, ὡς ἀπό γε τῆς συνηθείας τῆς ἐπὶ τῶν μυιῶν. Ἐν ἔθει γάρ πώς ἐστι τοῖς μελισσοκόμοις συρίζειν αὐταῖς· οὕτω τε τῶν σίμβλων ἀποφέρειν εἰς ἄνθη, καὶ πόας, καὶ μὴν καὶ ἀνακομίζειν ἐξ ἀγρῶν, οἴκοί τε αὐτὰς ἐναυλίζεσθαι ποιεῖν. [Dechetai de kai touto palin, hōs apo ge tēs synētheias tēs epi tōn myiōn. En ethei gar pōs esti tois melissokomois syrizein autais; houtō te tōn simblōn apopherein eis anthē, kai poas, kai mēn kai anakomizein ex agrōn, oikoi te autas enaulizesthai poiein.] He takes this again as if from the habit of flies (that is, of bees). For beekeepers are accustomed to hiss at them, and so to lead them out of the hives to flowers and herbs, and to call them back from the fields, and to make them stay at home. Others use the ringing of brass, or potsherds struck together, for the same purpose. Columella, book 9, ch. 8, §10: If (the swarm) is hidden in a cave, it will be drawn out with smoke; and when it has burst out, it is checked by the clashing of brass. And ch. 12: Let the fleeing young swarm be frightened with brass rattles, or with the sound of potsherds, which usually lie about everywhere. Pliny, book 11, ch. 20: They delight in clapping and the ringing of brass, and are called together by it. From which it is clear that they also have the sense of hearing. Aelian, book 5, ch. 13: Ὅταν γοῦν σκιρτήσωσιν, καὶ πλανηθῶσιν, ἐνταῦθα οἱ σμηνουργοὶ κροτοῦσι [III, 359] κρότον τινὰ ἐμμελῆ τε, καὶ συμμελῆ. αἱ δὲ ὡς ὑπὸ σειρῆνος ἕλκονται, καὶ μέντοι ὑποστρέφουσιν εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα αὖθις. [Hotan goun skirtēsōsin, kai planēthōsin, entautha hoi smēnourgoi krotousi kroton tina emmelē te, kai symmelē. hai de hōs hypo seirēnos helkontai, kai mentoi hypostrephousin eis ta oikeia authis.] When they frolic and stray, the beekeepers then make a melodious and harmonious sound. And they are drawn back as if by a Siren, and return to their accustomed homes. Virgil:
Raise a ringing, and shake the cymbals of Mars around;
that is, so that you may call the wandering bees back to the hives. And a little later, when they go out to battle:
— — — — — the laggards that Martial blare of hoarse brass rebukes, and a voice is heard imitating the broken blasts of trumpets.
And again:
Following the sound of the Curetes and the clashing brass, they fed the king of heaven beneath the Dictaean cave.
Ovid, on Bacchus, book 3 of the Fasti, line 739:

And now they had come to Rhodope and the Pangaean streams, when the brass-bearing hands of his companions clashed. Behold! new winged creatures gather, driven by the ringing, and the bees follow the brass whose sounds they hear.
Lucan, book 9, line 288:
— — as when the sound of Phrygian brass rings out, astonished, they cease their flight, and return to their eager flower-gathering labour and the love of sacred honey.
Claudian, Panegyric on the sixth Consulship of Honorius, line 259: [col. 507]
— — — as the old Hyblaean man, shaking from afar the Cybelean brass, tries with the ringing to recall the fugitive bees, which of their own accord have deserted and left their honeycombs. — — — —

Didymus, Geoponica book 15 [ch. 3, §. 7]: Θέλγει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ζῶον, καὶ κάλλιστον μέλος· ὅθεν οἱ μελισσουργοὶ διασκορπιζομένας αὐτὰς κυμβαλίζοντες, ἢ τὰς χεῖρας εὐρύθμως κροτοῦντες συνάγουσι· [Thelgei de touto to zōon, kai kalliston melos; hothen hoi melissourgoi diaskorpizomenas autas kymbalizontes, ē tas cheiras eurythmōs krotountes synagousi] This animal is also charmed by the sweetness of song. Hence beekeepers gather scattered bees by striking cymbals or clapping their hands in rhythm. Against these the Philosopher is cited in vain, as though in the first book of the Physics he asserted that bees lack hearing. For I find the passage they cite nowhere. Indeed, in History book 9, ch. 40, he says that they are roused to work in the morning by a sound, and in the evening are called back from work by another sound, so that they may settle down [III, 360] to rest. Ὄρθριαι, he says, σιωπῶσιν, ἕως ἂν μία ἐγείρῃ βομβήσασα δὶς, ἢ τρίς· τότε δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἔργον ἀθροαὶ πέτονται· καὶ ἐλθοῦσαι πάλιν, θορυβοῦσι τὸ πρῶτον. κατὰ μικρὸν δ᾽ ἧττον, ἕως ἂν μία περιπετομένη βομβήσῃ ὥσπερ σημαίνουσα καθεύδειν· εἶτ᾽ ἐξαπίνης σιωπῶσι· [Orthriai … siōpōsin, heōs an mia egeirē bombēsasa dis, ē tris; tote d' ep' ergon athroai petontai; kai elthousai palin, thorybousi to prōton. kata mikron d' hētton, heōs an mia peripetomenē bombēsē hōsper sēmainousa katheudein; eit' exapinēs siōpōsi] In the morning they are silent until one rouses them by buzzing twice or three times. Then they fly out to work all together. When they return, they at first make a din, but gradually less and less, until one, flying around, buzzes as if giving the signal to sleep; and from then on they are at once silent. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 10: At night they rest until morning, when one rouses them with a double or triple buzz, as with a trumpet. Likewise: When evening comes, they hum in the hive less and less, until one flies around with the same buzz with which it roused them, as if ordering them to take rest, and this in the manner of a military camp. Then suddenly all fall silent. Yet, to state the matter as it is, the Philosopher had shortly before left the question uncertain in these words: Δοκοῦσι δὲ χαίρειν αἱ μέλιτται καὶ τῷ κρότῳ. διὸ καὶ κροτοῦντές φασιν ἀθροίζειν αὐτὰς εἰς τὸ σμῆνος, ὀστράκοις τε, καὶ ψόφοις. ἔστι μέν τοι ἄδηλον ὅλως, εἴτε ἀκούουσιν, εἴτε μὴ, καὶ πότερον· ἢ δι᾽ ἡδονὴν τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν, ἢ διὰ φόβον. [Dokousi de chairein hai melittai kai tō krotō. dio kai krotountes phasin athroizein autas eis to smēnos, ostrakois te, kai psophois. esti men toi adēlon holōs, eite akouousin, eite mē, kai poteron; ē di' hēdonēn touto poiousin, ē dia phobon] Bees also seem to delight in clapping. For this reason they are said to be gathered into the hive by the sound of brass or earthenware. Yet it is entirely uncertain whether they hear, and which of the two is the case: whether they do this from pleasure or from fear ^{R4}.

In Deut 1:44 Moses says of the Amorites, whom the Israelites had found the most hostile of all the Canaanites: They pursued you כאשר תעשינה דבורים, as bees do. So most of the ancients. But the Syriac renders it very differently: They pursued you, as bees ܡܬܬܢܢܢ [מתתננן] that are smoked (or provoked by smoke) pursue an intruder. And the Arabic manuscript which I saw in Sweden: فطردوكم كما يطرد النحل بالدخان [fa-ṭaradūkum kamā yuṭrad al-naḥl bi-l-dukhān] And they drove you out, as bees are driven out by smoke. The Chaldee Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] too should be read thus: כמא דיתנן דבריתא, as one who smokes bees. For the word דנתון, which they twist in various ways, admits no suitable sense. These translators, evidently, seem to have read instead of תעשינה thaasena, that is, they do, תעשנה theassenna, that is, they are smoked: a slight change in the letters, and not an unsuitable sense. For it is well known that those who take the honey from hives first drive the bees off with smoke. Hence the poet, Georgics book 4, line 230:

— — and hold out in your hand pursuing smoke. [III, 361] And there Servius: Also bring smoke, so that, when the bees have withdrawn, frightened by these things, you may gather the honey with impunity. Likewise: Pursuing smoke, that is, the pursuers of the bees, as in and Malea's pursuing waves. And Ovid, De remedio Amoris book 1, line 185:
What of when swarms flee the smoke set beneath them, so that the honeycombs, removed, may lighten the curved wickerwork?
And Zonas, on Pan, to the bees, Anthology book 1, ch. 60:
— — — ὁ δὲ βλυστηρίδι χειρὶ [col. 508] Καπνώσας, βαίην κὔμμι λίπῃ μερίδα. [ho de blystēridi cheiri kapnōsas, baiēn kymmi lipē merida]
But may he, raising smoke with his honey-taking hand, leave you a small portion (of the honey). And of Aristaeus, Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 5, line 249:
Καὶ δολίῳ πνιγόεντι πυρὸς τεχνήμονι καπνῷ Σινομένην πρήϋνεν· — — — [Kai doliō pnigoenti pyros technēmoni kapnō sinomenēn prēynen]

And with the crafty, choking, skilful smoke of fire he calmed the harmful (bee). There are others too who report the same. Antigonus, History of Marvels 37: Τὰς δὲ μελίττας θυμιωμένας ὑπὸ τοῦ καπνοῦ, καὶ κακοπαθούσας τότε μάλιστα μὲν ἐσθίειν· [Tas de melittas thymiōmenas hypo tou kapnou, kai kakopathousas tote malista men esthiein] Bees (they say), when they are fumigated with smoke and harassed, then eat most of all. The Scholiast of Aristophanes, on these words of the Poet in the Wasps:
— — — Τῦφε πολλῷ τῷ καπνῷ, [Typhe pollō tō kapnō]

Kindle it with much smoke. Τῦφε δὲ καίων δίωκε· ὁ γαρ καπνὸς διώκει τὰς μελισσας, καὶ τὰς σφῆκας [Typhe de kaiōn diōke; ho gar kapnos diōkei tas melissas, kai tas sphēkas]. The word τῦφε [typhe] means: Burning, pursue: for smoke pursues bees and wasps. Columella, book 9, chapter 15, §5, where he speaks of taking the honey from beehives: When the hive has been opened at the back, where there is no entrance, we shall apply smoke made from galbanum, or from dry smoke (perhaps hay) ^{R5}. And below: The smoke is driven toward the bees, which at once, unable to bear the reek, betake themselves to the front part of their dwelling, and sometimes outside the entrance. Pliny, book 11, ch. 16: When the honey is taken out, it is most useful to drive the bees off with smoke, so that they do not become angry or greedily devour it themselves. With more frequent smoke their sluggishness is also roused to work. In Greek this is called βλίσαι [blisai] and ἐναύειν [enauein]. Hesychius: Βλίσαι· [III, 362] καπνίσαι μελίσσας, καὶ ἐξελάσαι τῶν σκηνῶν [Blisai; kapnisai melissas, kai exelasai tōn skēnōn] (read σμηνῶν [smēnōn]). To fumigate bees and drive them out of their hives. Likewise, ἐναύοντες· ἀνάπτοντες πυρί. τὰ γὰρ σμήνη τῶν μελισσῶν διώκουσι διὰ πυρὸς καὶ καπνοῦ [enauontes; anaptontes pyri. ta gar smēnē tōn melissōn diōkousi dia pyros kai kapnou]: Kindling fire: for they pursue swarms of bees with fire and smoke. And in Arabic جلا [jalā] giala. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: جلا النحل دخن عليها ليشتار العسل [jalā al-naḥl dakhkhana ʿalayhā li-yashtār al-ʿasal] Giala the bee, that is, he fumigated it, in order to take the honey out of the hive. In the Talmud, tractate Kelim, ch. 16, §7, p. 26a, the Glossator explains what מדף של דבורים, the maddaph of bees, is, as follows: כלי שמשימין בו אש וגללי בקר ומעשנים שיברחו מן הכוורת הנחילים ויקח הדבש מלשון אשר תדפנו רוח, It is a vessel in which fire and cow dung are placed, by whose fumigation the bees are put to flight from the hive, so that the honey may be taken (it is derived from the verb נדף, to drive away): whence Ps 1:4: “The wind drives it away.” From this fumigation, moreover, the poets everywhere draw similes, as Moses does in this passage, if we follow the Syriac, Chaldee and Arabic versions. Lycophron on Paris, line 180:

Χ' ὡμὲν παλιμπόρευτον ἵξεται τρίβον, Σφῆκας δαφοινὲς χηράμων ἀνειρύσας, Ὁποῖα κοῦρος δῶμα κινήσας καπνῷ· [Ch' hōmen palimporeuton hixetai tribon, Sphēkas daphoines chēramōn aneirysas, Hopoia kouros dōma kinēsas kapnōi;]
And he indeed will go back by the way he came, drawing blood-red wasps out of their holes, as when a boy has smoked out a hive.
That is, having carried off Helen and returning to Troy, he will provoke the Greeks, as wasps and bees are provoked by smoke. And at line 254 the same poet says of the Greeks:
Ἀλλ' ὡς μέλισσαι συμπεφυρμέναι καπνῷ. [All' hōs melissai sympephyrmenai kapnōi.]
But like bees mingled with smoke, etc. See the rest there. Apollonius, Argonautica book 2, line 29:

Λευγαλέως Βέβρυκας ὑπερφιάλους ἐφόβησαν· Ὡς δὲ μελισσάων σμῆνος μέγα μηλοβοτῆρες, Ἠὲ μελισσοκόμοι, πέτρῃ ἔνι καπνιόωσιν· Αἱ δή τοι τείως μὲν ἀολλέες ᾧ ἐνὶ σίμβλῳ Βομβηδὸν κλονέονται, ἐπιπρὸ δὲ λιγνυόεντι Καπνῷ τυφόμεναι πέτρης ἑκὰς ἀΐσσουσιν. [Leugaleōs Bebrykas hyperphialous ephobēsan; Hōs de melissaōn smēnos mega mēlobotēres, Ēe melissokomoi, petrēi eni kapnioōsin; Hai dē toi teiōs men aollees hōi eni simblōi Bombēdon kloneontai, epipro de lignyoenti Kapnōi typhomenai petrēs hekas aïssousin.]

They sorely terrified the arrogant Bebryces, as shepherds or beekeepers fumigate a great swarm of bees in a rock. These meanwhile, crowded together in their hive [col. 509] , are thrown into confusion with a buzzing, but, scorched beyond measure by the sooty smoke, they pour out far from the rock. Here the Scholiast writes that bees flee smoke διὰ τὸ στενόπωρον [III, 363] εἶναι αὐτῶν τὴν ὄσφρησιν [dia to stenopōron einai autōn tēn osphrēsin], because their organs of smell have very narrow passages. Virgil, of the people of Lavinium besieged in their city by Aeneas, Aeneid book 12:

Others bear arms and press on to defend the walls: as when a shepherd has tracked bees shut up in a hollow rock and filled it with bitter smoke. They within, alarmed for their safety, run to and fro through their waxen camp and whet their anger with loud buzzing. The black reek rolls through the dwelling; now the rocks within resound with a hidden murmur, and the smoke goes up into the empty air.
Quintus Smyrnaeus, on Ajax defending the carcass of Achilles against the Trojans, book 3, line 217:

— — τοὶ δ᾽ οὐκ ἀπέληγον ὁμοκλῆς, Ἀλλὰ οἱ ἀμφεμάχοντο, περισταδὸν ἀΐσσοντες, Αἰὲν ἐπασσύτεροι, τανυχειλέες εὖτε μέλισσαι, Αἵθ᾽ ἑὸν περὶ σίμβλον ἀπειρέσιαι ποτέωνται, ῎Ανδρ᾽ ἀπαμυνόμεναι, ὃδ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἐκ ἀλέγων ἐπιούσας, Κηροὺς ἐκτάμνησι μελίχροας· αἳ δ᾽ ἀκάχωνται Καπνοῦ ὑπαὶ ῥιπῆς ἠ δ᾽ ἀνέρος· ἀλλ᾽ ἄρα καὶ ὡς Ἀντίαι ἀΐσσουσιν, ὃ δ᾽ οὐκ ὄθετ᾽, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα βαιόν. [— — toi d' ouk apelēgon homoklēs, Alla hoi amphemachonto, peristadon aïssontes, Aien epassyteroi, tanycheilees eute melissai, Haith' heon peri simblon apeiresiai poteōntai, Andr' apamynomenai, hod' ar' ek alegōn epiousas, Kērous ektamnēsi melichroas; hai d' akachōntai Kapnou hypai rhipēs ē d' aneros; all' ara kai hōs Antiai aïssousin, ho d' ouk othet', oud' ara baion.]

They did not cease their threats, but attacked him, rushing in from all sides ever more thickly, like long-lipped bees that fly in countless swarms around their hive to ward off a man (gathering the honey). He, however, paying no heed to their onset, cuts out the honeyed combs. And they, although tormented by the onslaught of the smoke and of the man, still press against him. But he takes not the least account of them. Gregory of Nazianzus, in the Poem On his own life:
᾽Ανίστατ᾽ εὐθὺς ὥσπερ ἐκ καπνοῦ βίας ᾽Εσμὸς μελισσῶν· — — — [Anistat' euthys hōsper ek kapnou bias Hesmos melissōn; — — —]
At once (the people) rises up like a swarm of bees under the force of smoke.

Now that we have dealt fully with smoke, it remains for us to speak of the bravery of bees, with reference to those passages of Scripture in which the most hostile enemies are compared with bees: as above, the Amorites, of whom Moses says, And they pursued you, as bees do. And in Ps 118:12 David says of his enemies, They surrounded me like bees. And in Isa 7:18 The Lord will hiss for the bee that is in the land of Assur. There the Chaldee has: The Lord will call to the mighty forces, דאנון תקיפין כדבריתא, which are strong like bees, and he will bring them from the borders of the land of Assyria. And in the same place R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], [III, 364] לדבורה חיל גבורים דעוקצים כדבורים, To the bee, that is, to an army of mighty men who sting like bees. Lest these comparisons should seem to fall below the dignity of the subject, it must be understood that the bee has a great spirit in so slight a little body; and that, to protect their honey, bees do not fear to attack with their hostile stings not only men but even all the largest animals, and sometimes they kill them. Aristotle, History, book 9, ch. 40: Κτείνουσι δὲ βάλλουσαι καὶ τὰ μεγάλα τῶν ζώων. καὶ ἵππος ἤδη ἀπέθανεν ὑπὸ μελιττῶν [Kteinousi de ballousai kai ta megala tōn zōōn. kai hippos ēdē apethanen hypo melittōn]. By driving in their sting they kill all the largest animals. Indeed, a horse once died from being stung by bees. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 18: There are instances of horses killed by them. Moreover, Aelian, book 17, ch. 35, reports from Antenor that the Rhaucians, a people of Crete, were driven out of their city by the stings of χαλκοειδῶν [chalkoeidōn] bees and migrated elsewhere. It is no wonder, then, if the same creatures proved fatal to Hermonax, a boy, of whom Antipater writes in book 1 of the Anthology, ch. 37:
Τὸ βρέφος Ἑρμάνακτα διεχρήσασθε μέλισσαι, [To brephos Hermanakta diechrēsasthe melissai,]
You killed the infant Hermonax, bees. And Bianor:
Κοῦρον ἀποπλανίην, ἐπιμάζιον, Ἑρμώνακτα Φεῦ! βρέφος ὡς ἀδίκως εἵλετε βουγενέες; [Kouron apoplaniēn, epimazion, Hermōnakta / Pheu! brephos hōs adikōs heilete bougenees?]
The wandering, suckling boy Hermonax, an infant, alas! how unjustly you destroyed him, bees! Accordingly, in Theocritus, Idyll 19, Cupid the κηριοκλέπτης [kēriokleptēs] complains to his mother
— — — — ὅττι γε τυτθὸν [col. 510] Θηρίον ἐντὶ μέλισσα, καὶ ἁλίκα τραύματα ποιεῖ· [— — — — hotti ge tytthon / Thērion enti melissa, kai halika traumata poiei;]

That though the bee is so tiny a little creature, it inflicts such great wounds. Swarms of bees have also often been of use in war. Thus in Appian's Mithridatic Wars, when the troops of Lucullus were attacking Themiscyra through tunnels, the Themiscyrans sent bears and other wild beasts, and σμήνη μελισσῶν [smēnē melissōn], swarms of bees, against the workmen. And when Amurath was besieging Alba Graeca, the townspeople defended themselves by letting loose swarms of bees on the Turks, as Bonfinius writes in Decade 3, book 4. Not unlike this is what Widukind reports in book 1 of On the Deeds of the Saxons: one of the commanders of the Emperor Henry, besieged by Giselbert, king of Lotharingia, held back the attackers by throwing beehives at them; the horses, driven to frenzy by the stings, either threw their riders or made them useless for fighting. And in the year 1513, when Barriga, a Portuguese commander, had reduced Tanli, a town of the Moors in the territory of Xiatima, almost to the last extremity, the townspeople, seeing themselves brought into the utmost danger, set on fire countless beehives, of which they had great plenty, and let them down from the walls. Our men, both scorched by the flames of the hives and goaded by the stings of the bees, were forced to abandon the assault. These are the words of Osorius, book 8, On the Deeds of Emmanuel. Therefore, if not true, [III, 365] it is at least plausible, what Iamblichus writes in Photius about the forces besieging Rhodanes and Sinonis: Φεύγουσιν ὁ στρατὸς, τῷ τῶν μελισσῶν πολέμῳ πονούμενοι [Pheugousin ho stratos, tō tōn melissōn polemō ponoumenoi]. The forces flee, distressed by the attack of the bees ^{R5}. Nor is it altogether incredible, what we cited above from Herodotus, that certain regions beyond the Ister were inaccessible to men because of the multitude of bees. Today, among the penalties that the Jewish nation imposes on an adulterer, one is that he must pass naked in summer through a dense crowd of bees and expose his body to their stings until he is swollen all over; and after he has recovered, he must undergo the same penalty again, or even more often, according to the gravity of the sin. So it is stated in ch. 34 of Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum]'s Synagoga.

notes.text: J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] Hebrr. vol. 2, p. 388, holds that the name דבורה was given to bees from pursuing, since scarcely any other animal is fiercer in pursuit. This etymology would be apt enough, if only the verb דבר meant to pursue. For Michaelis takes the Piel conjugation of that verb in this sense at 2 Chr 22:10, and renders the whole passage ותדבר את כל זרע הממלכה thus: she pursued, namely to destruction, all the royal seed. This seems to be rejected if only because the verb nowhere else in the O. T. occurs in that sense, nor does that notion suit any passage; [III, 353] not to mention that in none of the languages cognate with Hebrew is this verb used in that sense. The etymology proposed by Bochart is therefore preferable, and Storr also approved it in Observatt. ad Anal. et Syntax. Hebr. p. 5, note. Michaelis rightly observes, however, that the Syriac ܕܒܘܪܐ [דבורא] is a somewhat broader name than the Hebrew, also covering wasps and hornets, and is used for the Hebrew צרעה at Exod 23:28. Deut 7:20. Josh 24:12.

Nymph. p. 104; and Niclas on the Geopon. book 15, ch. 2, §§ 14, 24, p. 1064 and 1070.

notes.text: It does not, however, seem necessary to understand ימים in the story of Samson as the space of a year, since in those regions the heat of the sun so dries out carcasses within a few days that only the framework of the bones, covered with hide, remains, as Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] rightly observes in Vermischten Sammlungen, part 6, Chapter 20, p. 135 f., German trans.

notes.text: Nor has anyone yet been able to find organs of hearing in bees. Oedmann, loc. cit., therefore thinks that the Hebrew poet at Isa 5:26 and VII, 18. means only this in general: that the countless armies of Assyria would be ready at a nod to inflict on the Israelites the punishments announced by Jehovah.

notes.text: Rather: with dung, as Palladius also has it (who follows Columella so closely that he seems to have compiled his writings), De re rustica, book 7, ch. 7, § 2: smoke is applied from galbanum and dry cow dung. Didymus in the Geoponica, book 15, Chapter 4, § 6: Ἠρινῶν δε δεκα ἡμερων διελθουσων, καπνῳ βολβιτου ξηρου ἐπι τας νομας αὐτας ἐξελασας, καθαρισεις και κορησεις τα ἀγγεια [Ērinōn de deka hēmerōn dielthousōn, kapnō bolbitou xērou epi tas nomas autas exelasas, kathariseis kai korēseis ta angeia]. But after ten days of spring have passed, you will drive them out to pasture with the smoke of dry cow dung, and you will clean and sweep the vessels. The same, Chapter 5, § 5: Χρη δε καπνῳ βολβιτου προαπολαυνειν αὐτας [Chrē de kapnō bolbitou proapolaunein autas].
